item.title: Operator-Adapted Multiscale Kernels for High-Contrast Elliptic Inverse Problems
item.description: arXiv:2611.10071v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider the joint recovery of the state and diffusion coefficient in a high-contrast elliptic equation from sparse, noisy state measurements. We seek the coefficient in a parameterized family defined relative to a prescribed reference coefficient. We construct a generalized multiscale finite element basis from the reference coefficient and use it to define a finite-rank kernel for the state. A weak Galerkin residual enforces the equation without pointwise differentiation across material interfaces. For each trial coefficient, the state is obtained by solving a linear least-squares problem. Variable projection eliminates the state coordinates from the objective, and the reduced gradient is evaluated without an adjoint PDE solve. We split the state reconstruction error into multiscale approximation, penalty relaxation, and parameter estimation terms. Under an admissible patch decomposition, the squared multiscale approximation error is bounded by a local spectral tail estimate with a contrast-independent interpolation constant. For a fixed coefficient and discretization, the penalty relaxation error is of order $O(\varepsilon^2)$ when the residual weight is proportional to $\varepsilon^{-2}$. The parameter contribution is bounded by local Lipschitz continuity of the projected state. In 50 synthetic tests based on a reference medium of contrast $10^4$, the multiscale space with the weak residual gives mean relative state and log-coefficient errors of 2.37\% and 4.43\%, respectively, the lowest among the four configurations tested.
item.dc:creator: Siqing Liu, Eric Chung

item.title: Laplace approximation of the parameter posterior with embedded error for efficient uncertainty quantification of expensive model calibrations
item.description: arXiv:2611.10210v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In practical engineering, there is a clear need for uncertainty quantification (UQ) of models used in design because forward UQ puts probabilities on performance predictions. However, without surrogate building, most forward engineering models are too expensive for traditional UQ methods like Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling. Our goal is to provide inexpensive, approxi- mate UQ that can be applied after an expensive traditional least squares fit, where the UQ handles both uncorrelated noise and parameter variance as in the embedded-error treatment developed by Sargsyan, Najm, and Ghanem (2015). After developing the basic theory to connect a Laplace-like approximation to Bayesian calibration, we compare the proposed method to black-box variational inference in terms of cost and fidelity. Then we demonstrate the method on real-world calibration of solid material models.
item.dc:creator: Reese E. Jones, Kyle N. Karlson, Matt W. Kury, Moe Khalil, Ray S. Tuminaro

item.title: Convergence of Adaptive Least Squares Finite Element Methods
item.description: arXiv:2611.10278v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider a general class of operator equations $\mathcal B u=f$ where $\mathcal B:\mathbb U\to \mathbb L_2$ is a linear isomorphis from a Hilbert space $\mathbb U$ onto an ``$L_2$-type'' space $\mathbb L_2 = L_2(\Omega;\mathbb R^q)$. This covers weak first order formulations of stationary elliptic boundary value problems, the Stokes system or systems for linear elasticity as well as space-time formulations of heat or wave equations. Since an $L_2$-residual is uniformly equivalent to the corresponding error in the trial space norm reliable and efficient computable a posteriori error bounds are for free. In contrast to a matured theory of classical adaptive finite element methods, estblishing linear convergence - and eventually optimal complexity - in a least squares setting seems to have remained open. To a large extent this is due to the fact that least squares error indicators do not exhibit any explicit dependence on local mesh-sizes. In this paper we propose a rather different approach to establish under which circumstances standard D\"orfler-marking mesh refinement gives rise to linear convergence and rate optimality of adaptive least squares finite element methods as well. A central role is played by a new notion of {\em data-visibility} which is a structural property of the data rather than a smoothness condition.
item.dc:creator: Wolfgang Dahmen

item.title: How good are spline spaces for the Kolmogorov $n$-width of a Sobolev ball?
item.description: arXiv:2611.10371v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper studies the approximation power of polynomial splines on a uniform one-dimensional mesh. The quality of the best approximation of the unit ball of $H^{s}$ by an $n$-dimensional subspace, measured in the $L^{2}$ norm, is quantified by the sup-inf of that space: for each function in the Sobolev ball, take its minimal approximation error over the space, and then take the supremum of these errors over the ball. The infimum of this sup-inf over all $n$-dimensional spaces is the well-known Kolmogorov $n$-width $d_{n}$. Choosing the $n$-dimensional subspace to be the piecewise polynomial space of degree $k$ with smoothness $C^{\mu}$ ($-1\le\mu\le k-1$) gives our sup-inf $E$. The approximation accuracy of spline spaces is then examined by comparing $d_{n}$ and $E$. The two quantities are determined by two eigenvalue problems, through which we obtain a lower bound for $d_{n}$ and an upper bound for $E$. Under the restriction $k\ge s-1$, the upper bound for the error of the maximally smooth spline space ($\mu=k-1$) is asymptotically equal to the lower bound for $d_n$, showing that uniform $B$-splines are asymptotically optimal among all $n$-dimensional spaces. For $\mu<k-1$, we prove that $E/d_n$ is bounded below by a constant strictly larger than $1$, except when $k>s-1$ and $\mu=k-2$ hold simultaneously. This reveals the superiority of $B$-splines in the sense of $n$-widths. Numerical experiments corroborate these bounds and, in some cases (e.g. the exception above), show that they are sharp.
item.dc:creator: Peng Yang, Zhimin Zhang

item.title: High-order long-time stable methods for the forced incompressible Navier--Stokes equations
item.description: arXiv:2611.10436v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present in this paper two scalar auxiliary variable (SAV) correction steps for constructing long-time stable schemes for the forced incompressible Navier--Stokes equations with no-slip boundary conditions. A main feature is that the same correction steps apply to any linear predictor satisfying the order and spatial regularity requirements in Assumption~P. Their construction and stability analysis are independent of the particular form of the predictor and require no energy estimate for it. The first correction uses a damped, shifted kinetic-energy variable to obtain a uniform-in-time $L^2$ bound in two and three dimensions, together with a weighted dissipation estimate. In two dimensions, the second correction combines a higher-energy auxiliary variable with a scalar relaxation to yield a uniform-in-time $H^1$ bound. Under the stated assumptions, these estimates hold on arbitrary positive time grids, without restrictions on step sizes or adjacent step ratios. We also derive eventual absorbing bounds; for the two-SAV scheme, these apply to the admissible initial class associated with fixed parameters. The generalized BDF schemes require one constant-coefficient Helmholtz solve per velocity component and one pressure Poisson solve per step; the second correction adds no field solve. Numerical experiments exhibit second-, third-, and fourth-order convergence for the tested BDF schemes and illustrate the long-time stability and efficiency of adaptive time stepping.
item.dc:creator: Fukeng Huang, Jie Shen, Xiaoming Wang

item.title: A Trajectory-Aware Domain-Decomposed Multispace Reduced Basis Preconditioner for Parametric Helmholtz Problems
item.description: arXiv:2611.10491v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Repeated solutions of parametric Helmholtz problems arise in multi-query applications such as sensitivity analysis and uncertainty quantification. Classical preconditioned iterative solvers do not automatically reuse low-dimensional structures across parameters. Multispace reduced basis (MSRB) preconditioners can exploit such structures by constructing iteration-specific reduced order models (ROMs) from training data, but storing global iteration-dependent bases incurs substantial memory costs. Building on trajectory-aware MSRB training, we develop a domain-decomposed MSRB (DD-MSRB) preconditioner for parametric Helmholtz systems truncated by perfectly matched layers (PMLs). Within flexible GMRES, each reduced space is trained on inverse-action snapshots along the Krylov trajectories generated by the ROM-based preconditioners applied in preceding iterations. To reduce storage, problem-adapted spatial partitions exploit heterogeneous local snapshot compressibility across the physical interior and the PML. Local basis dimensions in each subdomain are determined greedily under a global snapshot-error budget to balance approximation accuracy and storage. The resulting hybrid solver applies DD-MSRB preconditioning during the initial iterations to capture dominant cross-parameter modes and then switches, when necessary, to a shifted-Laplacian preconditioner to reduce error components poorly represented by the reduced spaces. Numerical experiments on two-dimensional half-space propagation, elliptic-obstacle scattering, and three-dimensional waveguides demonstrate significant acceleration over the shifted-Laplacian baseline and substantial memory savings relative to global MSRB. For the largest waveguide system, with 11.0 million unknowns, DD-MSRB reduces deployed ROM storage by 44.9% and mean online solve time by 30.2% compared with global MSRB.
item.dc:creator: An Ping, Zhichao Peng, Pengliang Yang

item.title: Error Estimates and Convergence Analysis for Learning Mechanism--AI Coupled Dynamical Systems
item.description: arXiv:2611.10520v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Mechanism--AI coupled dynamical systems retain known mechanisms while learning unknown dynamics from data. We study how neural approximation, numerical integration, finite observations, and optimization jointly affect the accuracy of this learning process. For time-dependent learned terms in a fixed compact admissible class, we derive a four-component objective error bound within an optimal control formulation. Explicit estimates are obtained for constrained ReLU approximation and Euler integration, with deterministic quadrature and random sampling treated separately. Under joint refinement, we establish $\Gamma$-convergence of the approximate objectives and show that approximate minimizers approach the continuous optimal set when the global optimization gaps vanish. We also derive conditional stability estimates for state-dependent learned terms. Numerical experiments with a susceptible--infected--recovered (SIR) model illustrate the analysis and show how solver resolution affects continuous-trajectory accuracy even when training losses are similar.
item.dc:creator: Pengfei Song, Yanni Xiao, Yuan Lou, Shuangshuang Yin

item.title: A high-order structure-preserving ALE--SAV finite element method for moving contact line flows
item.description: arXiv:2611.10828v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a structure-preserving arbitrary Lagrangian--Eulerian (ALE) finite element method for incompressible Navier--Stokes flow with gravity and moving contact lines, based on a scalar auxiliary variable (SAV) reformulation. The reformulation expresses the geometric energy quadratically in the auxiliary variable and permits linear treatment of the capillary, wetting and gravitational forces. The method combines high-order isoparametric elements in space with a linearly implicit, second-order Crank--Nicolson discretization in time. Second-order extrapolation supplies the predicted geometry and known coefficients of the linear fluid--SAV system. Mesh motion changes the kinetic-energy inner product and requires a compatible discretization of the time-derivative terms in the ALE formulation. We discretize these terms using an $L^2$-isometric velocity transfer to retain the kinetic-energy balance after the geometry update. We also construct a boundary update that preserves area or volume exactly using only linear solves. The resulting scheme satisfies a discrete SAV energy-dissipation law and preserves area or volume exactly. Numerical experiments in two and three dimensions demonstrate high-order spatial and second-order temporal convergence and confirm SAV energy dissipation and area or volume conservation.
item.dc:creator: Shu Ma

item.title: Neural Operator Surrogates for Landweber Iteration in Solving Inverse Problems
item.description: arXiv:2611.10865v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Neural operators can accurately approximate well-posed mappings, but for unbounded or discontinuous operators, common in inverse problems, we verify that their network parameters often blow up in architectures such as DeepONet and FNO. To solve inverse problems stably, we use Landweber iteration, which requires only a forward map and the adjoint of its derivative (linearisation). To reduce repeated PDE forward evaluations, we replace the forward operator and its derivative with a differentiable neural-operator surrogate. We show that encoder-network-decoder operators, including generalised DeepONets and fully coupled Fourier operators, approximate both the forward map and its derivative. A modified discrepancy principle ensures decreasing error before finite stopping. With a compact preconditioner, the iterates remain in a compact set where accurate surrogates exist, and the stopped reconstructions converge as data and surrogate errors vanish under a regularity condition. We also relate the theory to derivative-informed training along finite directions, showing that the preconditioner determines which derivative errors affect the Landweber iteration update. Experiments on identifying a reaction coefficient in an elliptic equation show that smoothing reduces late-iteration deterioration for less accurate surrogates but slows sharp-feature recovery, and that smaller derivative errors along training directions do not by themselves improve reconstruction accuracy.
item.dc:creator: Kuo Gai, Marco A Iglesias, Shuai Lu, Frank Werner

item.title: DMP-Oriented Anisotropic Mesh Adaptation for SUPG Finite Element Methods for Time-Dependent Convection-Diffusion Problems
item.description: arXiv:2611.10963v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study discrete bound preservation for fully discrete piecewise-linear streamline upwind Petrov--Galerkin (SUPG) finite element approximations of time-dependent convection--diffusion equations on anisotropic triangular meshes. Although the continuous homogeneous-source problem satisfies a parabolic maximum principle, SUPG approximations can exhibit nonphysical undershoots and overshoots. We derive sufficient nodal discrete maximum principle (DMP) conditions that account for the stabilized mass matrix, the combined effects of physical and streamline diffusion, time-step restrictions, and transfer between successive meshes. The analysis identifies a SUPG-effective diffusion tensor and motivates an anisotropic metric aligned with its inverse. We construct a combined metric that retains the effective-tensor geometry while introducing solution-dependent mesh density through recovered Hessian information. The resulting DMP conditions provide a theoretical basis for anisotropic mesh design. Numerical experiments for time-dependent transport problems with isotropic and moderately anisotropic diffusion demonstrate that, under mass-compatible limited SUPG stabilization, the combined metric substantially reduces measured undershoots relative to other methods at matched nominal mesh budgets, although improved bound behavior can carry an accuracy penalty. A controlled tensor--density comparison in the anisotropic transport test supports a contribution from the effective tensor beyond the prescribed mesh density.
item.dc:creator: Xianping Li

item.title: On-the-Fly Reduced Bases Through the Lens of Augmented Krylov Methods
item.description: arXiv:2611.11129v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: On-the-fly reduced order models (ROMs) are widely used in applications where multiple queries of large-scale models are required in an iterative method, like PDE-constrained optimization or fluid-structure interaction. When compared to classical offline--online ROMs, they have the advantage of being agnostic to any precomputed training data, mesh or geometry, which makes them more general linear/nonlinear solver accelerators. The main goal of this work is to study the effect of using a reduced basis constructed on-the-fly to accelerate a restarted Krylov algorithm, and to formally bridge this category of data-driven methods with classical augmented Krylov methods. The guiding principles of on-the-fly reduced basis will be translated into the framework of Krylov subspace methods, for a Petrov-Galerkin projection method. Previous corrections generated by the algorithm are stored in a snapshot matrix, and a singular value decomposition (SVD) is used to determine a reduced subspace containing the most significant directions. It will be shown that this approach can be embedded in the framework of Krylov methods with augmented or deflated restart, but with a different, data-driven recycling strategy. An analytical study will be presented to determine the consequences of augmentation by ROM-based vectors. Numerical experiments on a convection-diffusion problem with various degrees of convection will show that the proposed methodology yields results comparable to classical iterative linear solvers in some regimes, especially for nearly symmetric or skew-symmetric operators. At equal sizes of the augmentation basis, the convergence was sometimes faster with the proposed framework than with deflation methods.
item.dc:creator: Philippe-Andr\'e Luneau

item.title: An Arbitrary-Order Distributional Finite Element Method for the Curl--Dev Grad Stokes System
item.description: arXiv:2611.11158v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop an arbitrary-order distributional finite element method for the three-dimensional curl--dev grad Stokes system governed by the Hessian complex. On tetrahedral meshes, the method couples degree-$(k+1)$ nonconforming symmetric-tensor virtual elements, degree-$k$ tangential-normal continuous traceless tensor elements, and Raviart--Thomas elements of index $k$, without additional virtual-element stabilization. Building on zero-extension curl--div theory, we derive a well-posed distributional saddle-point formulation with an $H(\operatorname{div})$ vector multiplier. A divergence-augmented discrete norm equivalence controls the full Raviart--Thomas space modulo translations and underpins mesh-uniform stability for each fixed $k\ge0$. We establish optimal $O(h^{k+1})$ energy error estimates and an optimal $O(h^{k+2})$ $L^2$ error estimate for the full symmetric-tensor approximation, under suitable regularity and load approximation assumptions. As an application, the method supplies the Stokes block of a decoupled triharmonic scheme with optimal Hessian error estimates. Numerical experiments support the predicted convergence rates for computable quantities.
item.dc:creator: Ziwen Gu, Xuehai Huang

item.title: A Discrete de Rham method for linear and nonlinear fourth-order plate models
item.description: arXiv:2611.11312v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop and analyze a Discrete de Rham (DDR) method for the Kirchhoff--Love plate problem on general polygonal meshes and demonstrate its extension to geometrically nonlinear plates. The construction uses local degrees of freedom and polynomial reconstructions, avoiding the implementation difficulties associated with globally $C^1$-conforming approximation spaces. A new deflection reconstruction obtained from the discrete Hessian permits a uniform treatment of the load term at all polynomial degrees. The use of this reconstruction improves the convergence rates of previous DDR methods and enables the formulation of a lowest-order scheme with only vertex unknowns. We provide a stability and convergence analysis of the method and validate the theoretical results through a comprehensive set of numerical tests. The method is then extended to the coupled von K\'arm\'an equations, for which we demonstrate convergence numerically. We also study the flat-branch spectrum of a compressed perforated plate and its small-amplitude forced nonlinear response near the first critical load.
item.dc:creator: Daniele A. Di Pietro, J\'er\^ome Droniou, Arax Leroy, Vito Patierno

item.title: A Geometry-Robust Ne\v{c}as-Type Inequality for Stokes Preconditioning
item.description: arXiv:2611.11442v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Pressure mass preconditioners for the incompressible Stokes equations can deteriorate on domains with narrow gaps. We develop a pressure preconditioner that uses the distance to the boundary to account for spatially varying geometric scales. Its application consists of a pressure mass solve and a weighted pressure Poisson solve, with the squared boundary distance as the diffusion coefficient. The theoretical basis is a distance-weighted pressure norm defined by splitting the pressure into an $L^2$ component and a component controlled by its weighted gradient. We prove that this norm is bounded by the negative norm of the pressure gradient on every bounded connected open set, with a constant depending only on the dimension. A reverse bound follows from the boundary Hardy inequality, giving norm equivalence uniformly over families with bounded Hardy constants. Two-dimensional finite element experiments on slender, perforated, and composite domains demonstrate stable performance across the tested geometric parameters and mesh refinements. The smallest eigenvalues of the preconditioned pressure Schur complement remain close to $0.54$, and block preconditioning with algebraic multigrid auxiliary solves requires about 20--30 FGMRES iterations across the geometric sweeps.
item.dc:creator: Qi Xin, Xie Yan, Shihua Gong

item.title: A DG method for the pseudostress-velocity formulation of the Stokes-Brinkman eigenvalue problem
item.description: arXiv:2611.11466v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce a discontinuous Galerkin method for the approximation of the eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of the Stokes-Brinkman eigenvalue problem. The method is based on a mixed formulation in which the pseudostress tensor and the fluid velocity are the main unknowns, while the pressure can be recovered through a post-processing procedure applied to the pseudostress tensor. Using discontinuous polynomial spaces of degree $k\geq 1$, we propose a consistent symmetric interior penalty discretization for the approximation of the spectrum. Relying on the spectral theory for non-compact operators, we establish convergence of the discrete spectral approximation and derive error estimates for the method. A series of numerical experiments is presented to assess its computational performance. On the one hand, we investigate the convergence rates for different polynomial degrees, computational domains, and values of the permeability. Furthermore, we study the influence of the stabilization parameter on the discrete spectrum by comparing different choices of this parameter and examining their impact on the occurrence of spurious eigenvalues.
item.dc:creator: Isabella Estrada, Felipe Lepe

item.title: A Legendre-Galerkin Method for Kinetic Models of Opinion Dynamics with Quasi-Invariant Consistency
item.description: arXiv:2611.11492v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Kinetic models of opinion dynamics provide a mesoscopic framework for describing collective behavior arising from interactions among a large number of individuals. Highly accurate numerical approximation to such Boltzmann-type equations, however, remains challenging due to the nonlinear inelastic collision operators involving multiple integrals coupling opinion variables and random perturbations. To address the difficulties, we develop a Legendre-Galerkin spectral method for a general class of kinetic models with opinion-dependent interaction rules. Our method exploits an exact decoupling of the weak collision kernel to obtain a time-independent tensor representation of the Galerkin collision operator. A recursive construction reduces collision-tensor assembly to one-dimensional quadrature, allowing the coefficients to be precomputed for subsequent use. A rigorous $L^2$-error estimate, along with mass preservation, is established for the fully discrete scheme under suitable regularity and stability assumptions. In the quasi-invariant regime, we derive the limiting Fokker-Planck equation and establish consistency between the exact Legendre-Galerkin operators of the rescaled Boltzmann equation and its limit for each fixed polynomial degree. Numerical experiments support the theoretical results, illustrate quasi-invariant consistency, and capture the formation of opinion clusters under the bounded-confidence interactions.
item.dc:creator: Rui Wang, Yunfeng Xiong

item.title: Suboptimality of Gaussian quadrature for Freud and logistic weights in weighted Sobolev spaces
item.description: arXiv:2611.11545v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the worst-case error of Gaussian quadrature for integrals over the real line weighted by Freud weights $\exp(-|x|^\beta)$ with $\beta>1$, and by the logistic density $\mathrm{e}^{-x}/(1+\mathrm{e}^{-x})^2$. The integrand functions are assumed to live in the $\rho$-weighted $L^2$-based Sobolev space of smoothness $\alpha\in\mathbb{N}$. We prove that any linear quadrature using the $n$ Gaussian nodes, irrespective of the choice of quadrature weights, has a worst-case error bounded from below by a constant times $n^{-\alpha(1-1/\beta)}$ for the Freud weights, and by a constant times $(\log n)^{-\alpha}$ for the logistic weight. Our proof is based on three simple observations. First, the worst-case error of any linear quadrature is bounded from below in terms of the number of its nodes in a fixed interval. Second, the number of Gaussian nodes in such an interval is bounded from above by means of Christoffel functions. Third, Christoffel functions admit sharp lower bounds on such an interval. For the Freud weights with even integer exponents and for the logistic weight, all steps are proved in an elementary and self-contained way; for the logistic weight, we use explicit recurrence coefficients of the corresponding orthogonal polynomials. Our results provide a theoretical explanation, for integrands of finite smoothness, of the slow convergence of Gauss--Logistic quadrature observed in the literature. In contrast, for the logistic weight and for the Freud weights with even integer exponents, the M\"obius-transformed trapezoidal rule attains the optimal rate $n^{-\alpha}$. This rule does not depend on the smoothness $\alpha$ and requires only point values of the integrand and the weight.
item.dc:creator: Yuya Suzuki

item.title: Optimal adaptive finite element methods in $W^{1,p}$
item.description: arXiv:2611.11668v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove linear convergence and algebraic rate optimality of an adaptive finite element method for the Dirichlet Poisson problem in W1p. We assume well-posedness of the continuous problem and discrete inf-sup stability over the refinement family. We verify both hypotheses when p is sufficiently close to 2, without requiring convexity of the domain. The Galerkin equations remain unchanged, while the residual estimator and D\"orfler marking use the target exponent p. Linear convergence holds for every fixed marking fraction between zero and one. For sufficiently small marking fractions and marked sets of nearly minimal cardinality, the method attains the best algebraic rates for W1p approximation together with data oscillation. The main ingredient is a Banach-space extension of Feischl's relaxed quasi-orthogonality, proved under discrete inf-sup stability.
item.dc:creator: Tsogtgerel Gantumur

item.title: An asymptotic preserving scheme for kinetic equations describing bacterial traveling pulses
item.description: arXiv:2611.11764v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider a kinetic model for bacterial chemotaxis that describes the propagation of traveling pulses driven by a nutrient and a self-produced chemoattractant. In the diffusive regime, the model converges to a macroscopic drift-diffusion system with bounded chemotactic fluxes. We construct a fully discrete asymptotic preserving (AP) finite difference scheme based on a micro-macro decomposition of the kinetic equation. The method is stable uniformly with respect to the scaling parameter and, as this parameter tends to zero, reduces to a consistent discretization of the limiting macroscopic equations. We prove positivity and mass conservation for the limiting scheme, and use a positivity-preserving correction for the kinetic solver. Numerical simulations reproduce the experimentally observed traveling pulses at both the kinetic and the macroscopic level, validate the theoretical traveling wave speed, and illustrate the convergence of the kinetic model to its macroscopic limit.
item.dc:creator: Canan Akkoyunlu, Jose A. Carrillo, Gissell Estrada-Rodriguez, Xinran Ruan

item.title: Structure-Informed Electromagnetic Feedback Control of the Vlasov-Maxwell System with Delayed Observations
item.description: arXiv:2611.11787v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Feedback control of kinetic plasma instabilities is challenging because observing the full phase-space distribution is costly, while sensing and actuation inevitably introduce delay. We develop a structure-informed electromagnetic feedback framework for the Vlasov-Maxwell system that uses only macroscopic observations to control the full kinetic distribution. We first show that magnetic actuation alone does not directly regulate radial velocity moments, motivating the use of combined electric and magnetic controls. A nonlinear perturbation estimate yields an instantaneous cancellation-dissipation feedback law. To account for delayed observations, we then use Maxwell's equations to identify the macroscopic quantities governing the resulting cancellation errors, namely currents and spatial field gradients. These quantities serve as inputs to a low-rank neural operator that learns a residual correction to the delayed cancellation baseline. Thus, while the feedback depends only on low-dimensional macroscopic observables, the control objective remains the stabilization of the full distribution toward a prescribed kinetic equilibrium. Numerical experiments for two-stream and Weibel-type instabilities demonstrate effective long-time stabilization under substantial feedback delays.
item.dc:creator: Jingcheng Lu, Li Wang

item.title: Operator Learning of Microstructure-Dependent Internal-Variable Models for Inelastic Homogenization: Approximation and Complexity
item.description: arXiv:2611.11805v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the learning of homogenized constitutive laws for inelastic heterogeneous materials, aiming to replace costly concurrent unit-cell simulations with surrogates that generalize across loading histories and microstructures. We focus on the recurrent neural operator framework, motivated by the explicit form of homogenized Kelvin--Voigt linear viscoelasticity. In this framework, internal variables enable a Markovian approximation of loading-history dependence, and neural operators represent the microstructure-dependent constitutive response. For periodic Kelvin--Voigt viscoelasticity, we prove a universal approximation theorem showing that the model can approximate the homogenized constitutive law to any prescribed accuracy, uniformly in time and over a wide set of admissible strain trajectories and microstructural property fields, in two and three dimensions. This comprises a significant extension of the existing, somewhat limited, one-dimensional theory that uses explicit solutions for piecewise constant materials. Instead, in two and three dimensions, we adopt a more versatile approximation based on the spectral representation of the memory kernel that arises from homogenization. This also enables us to give an explicit bound on the internal-variable dimension, sufficient for approximation, exhibiting logarithmic growth in the inverse relative stress error and in material contrast. Numerical experiments on viscoelasticity and crystal plasticity complement the theory, illustrating the roles of internal-variable dimension and sample complexity in learning homogenized responses from unit-cell data. Theoretical results are formally verified in Lean 4.
item.dc:creator: Lianghao Cao, George Stepaniants, Andrew M. Stuart

item.title: A Finite-Lag Markov Chain Model for Coarse-Graining Linear SDEs
item.description: arXiv:2611.12022v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we analyze a finite-lag Markov chain approximation for coarse-grained linear stochastic differential equations. The chain uses the limiting conditional transition law of the resolved variables to advance on a prescribed time grid. Its stability and statistical properties are studied, with particular attention to the role of the lag time. The chain preserves the exact equilibrium distribution and matches the autocovariance at the chosen lag, while errors at subsequent times are quantified. For a slow-fast system, the analysis relates lag selection to scale separation and dynamical accuracy. A continuous embedding of the chain enables a unified comparison with some existing continuous-time Markovian effective models based on the temporal statistics they preserve. Numerical examples illustrate the theoretical results.
item.dc:creator: Yuan Chen

item.title: Low-rank Low Precision Training of Gaussian Processes
item.description: arXiv:2611.12054v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Training Gaussian processes (GPs) at large scale is computationally challenging because evaluating the log-marginal likelihood and its gradients involves large, dense kernel matrices. We develop a scalable low-rank GP training approach that combines AnchorNet landmark selection with a fully independent training conditional (FITC) correction. The resulting objective and its analytic gradients can be evaluated using low-rank factors, diagonal quantities, and small dense matrices, without forming the full kernel matrix or its derivatives. The complete training procedure is implemented in single precision and evaluated on nine large-scale regression datasets. Across these problems, the method reaches the reference predictive accuracy while substantially reducing training time, although the required approximation rank varies across datasets. We also study the numerical behavior of the full-kernel predictive solve and show that single precision can become limiting for ill-conditioned problems. Finally, we investigate further reducing selected matrix operations to fp16 or TF32. These lower-precision variants provide only modest additional speedups and can become unreliable when the reduced system is poorly conditioned.
item.dc:creator: Moritz Poguntke, Eda Oktay, Yuanzhe Xi, Erin Carson, Martin Stoll

item.title: A Computational Brainsphere Model for the Simulation of Alzheimer's Disease
item.description: arXiv:2611.12084v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Nowadays, there are different medical imaging techniques to collect data about the progression of Alzhei\-mer's disease in a patient's brain. These data describe different phenomena which are still not understood from a biological point of view. How can these data sets be combined in a mathematical model to simulate the evolution of such a neurodegenerative disease in a computer? In this snapshot, we present one possible approach to address this task with the help of graph theory and partial differential equations.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Snapshots of modern mathematics from Oberwolfach;2026-07
item.dc:creator: Angela Kunoth, Anna Weller, Tolunay Yilmaz

item.title: Convergence of finite element exterior calculus for the Hodge-Dirac and Hodge-Laplace problems on closed Riemannian manifolds
item.description: arXiv:2611.12171v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove that the finite element exterior calculus (FEEC) approximation to the Hodge-Dirac and Hodge-Laplace problems on any closed oriented Riemannian manifold converges. Its approximate solutions, together with their exterior derivatives, converge to the continuum solutions for every source, and at the rate of the mesh size when the source and its codifferential are square integrable. We use Licht's estimate for the FEEC approximation of forms with one square-integrable derivative by finite element forms. We combine this with a new abstract error bound for approximations of Hilbert complexes. This bound uses a version of Di Pietro and Droniou's third Strang lemma. To apply these estimates, we show that every closed manifold admits a family of arbitrarily fine triangulations whose shapes stay uniformly under control.
item.dc:creator: Thomas A. Wasserman

item.title: Involution-Preserving schemes through constrained mesh motion: a novel Arbitrary-Lagrangian-Eulerian framework
item.description: arXiv:2611.12188v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce a novel structure-preserving finite volume method that exploits mesh motion to enforce differential involutions arising in hyperbolic systems of conservation laws. The key idea is to leverage the geometric degrees of freedom of an Arbitrary-Lagrangian-Eulerian (ALE) framework to construct a constrained mesh motion that is intrinsically compatible with the involution constraints embedded in the governing equations. The method is developed within a cell-centered formulation on moving quadrilateral meshes, where discrete divergence and curl operators are constructed from vertex-based differential operators. Particular care is devoted to the consistent evolution of the mesh geometry and the satisfaction of the Geometric Conservation Law (GCL). The proposed framework is applied to two representative hyperbolic systems featuring distinct involution constraints: the ideal magnetohydrodynamics equations, endowed with the divergence-free condition on the magnetic field, and the hyperbolic Euler-Heat equations, subject to a curl-free constraint on the thermal impulse. Second-order accuracy in time is achieved through a Runge-Kutta discretization, with the geometric constraints consistently enforced at each stage. A comprehensive set of classical benchmark problems is presented to assess the accuracy and effectiveness of the method. The numerical results demonstrate that appropriately constrained mesh motion provides an effective mechanism for preserving differential involutions, establishing a novel connection between mesh geometry and the structure-preserving discretization of hyperbolic systems.
item.dc:creator: Sacha Cardonna, Elena Bernardelli, Walter Boscheri

item.title: Unmasking shortcut solutions of coding agents on partial differential equations
item.description: arXiv:2611.12308v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Coding agents now write simulation programs, but benchmarks usually judge only whether their output matches a reference. In manufactured-solution tasks the data determine the exact solution, so a matching output need not come from a solver. We introduce PDEViBench, a benchmark of 290 tasks in six equation families that traces each passing program to the computation behind its output and reruns unclear programs on changed data. A Codex agent (GPT-5.2) passed 80% of 1,450 runs, yet about one pass in ten returned the exact solution without solving the equation. Counting only solved passes changed which task features made problems seem hard and reversed the ranking of two prompts. Once the prompt forbade the shortcut, every pass was a numerical solve, and on tasks without a closed-form solution passing programs stayed correct on changed data. Scientific coding benchmarks should check how each answer was computed as well as whether it matches.
item.dc:creator: Jiale Linghu, Yangshuai Wang

item.title: Reconstructing Flash-Evoked Potentials in the Human Brain and Tracking Cortical Activity Using Spatiotemporal Filtering: Numerical Simulation Study
item.description: arXiv:2611.12366v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Electroencephalographic source reconstruction of visual evoked activity is challenging because distributed, temporally evolving, and overlapping cortical sources generate scalp potentials. We present a controlled simulation framework for flash visual evoked potentials (FVEPs) based on a coupled Jansen--Rit neural mass network and a realistic finite-element EEG forward model. The framework generates a sequential activation pattern across early visual, parietal, and frontal regions and enables direct comparison of reconstructed activity with known ground truth. Standardized Kalman filtering (SKF), change-rate SKF (CrSKF), conventional Kalman filtering (KF), and linearly constrained minimum variance (LCMV) beamforming are compared using parcel-wise time courses, temporal lags, and assessments of spatial focality and Earth Mover's Distance. In the inverse comparison, SKF and CrSKF preserve the principal temporal progression more consistently than KF and LCMV, while CrSKF produces smoother temporal estimates. The results also demonstrate parcel-wise leakage and reduced separation of closely spaced components, emphasizing the need to interpret temporal ordering together with spatial reconstruction quality. The proposed framework provides a reproducible test environment for evaluating dynamic EEG inverse methods under controlled noise conditions.
item.dc:creator: Qiong Tao, Joonas Lahtinen, Sampsa Pursiainen

item.title: Total variation error bounds for Schr\"odinger-F\"ollmer samplers
item.description: arXiv:2611.12447v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sampling from high-dimensional, multimodal target distributions plays a fundamental role in scientific computing, statistics and machine learning. Recently, the Schr\"odinger-F\"ollmer sampler (SFS) has been proposed by Huang et al. (IEEE Trans. Inform. Theory, 2025) as an efficient sampling algorithm that transports the degenerate distribution at $t=0$ to the target distribution at $t=1$, without relying on long-time ergodicity. In this paper, we establish non-asymptotic error bounds for SFS in the total variation distance by deriving regularization estimates for the associated Kolmogorov equation via the Bismut-Elworthy-Li formula. When the drift can be computed exactly, a convergence rate of order $\mathcal{O}( h|\ln h|)$ was obtained under certain smoothness conditions on the drift with a uniform time step-size $h>0$. When the drift is approximated by Monte Carlo methods, we obtain a convergence rate of order $\mathcal{O}( h|\ln h|+ 1/M)$, where $M$ is the number of samples used in the Monte Carlo approximation. This yields a sharper dependence on $M$ than the existing bound $\mathcal{O}(1/\sqrt{M})$ in the $L^2$-Wasserstein distance in the aforementioned paper, by turning the total variation error to the weak error analysis in the setting of non-smooth test functions. Numerical experiments are presented to illustrate the convergence rate with respect to the time step-size $h$ and the Monte Carlo sample size $M$ and the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm.
item.dc:creator: Xiaojie Wang, Xiaoyan Zhang

item.title: VEM-bubble discretisation and iterative coupling algorithm for a fluid induced seismicity model with rate-and-state friction
item.description: arXiv:2611.12462v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This work addresses the discretisation and iterative coupling algorithm for an induced seismicity model accounting for fault reactivation and slip driven by subsurface fluid injection. The model couples single-phase Darcy flow in both the porous matrix and the fault network with a quasi-static poroelastic mechanical response in the bulk and fault slip governed by a rate-and-state friction law with radiation damping stabilisation leading to a quas-dynamic formulation. The contact mechanics problem is discretised using the Virtual Element Method with bubble stabilisation of the facewise constant Lagrange multiplier. It is combined with a Hybrid Finite Volume scheme for the mixed-dimensional Darcy flow model. The time discretisation is implicit and the nonlinear system is solved at each time step using an iterative coupling algorithm which iterates between the Darcy flow, the frictional contact-mechanics, and the state differential equation. The contraction of this iterative coupling algorithm is established with a smallness assumption on the time step independent on the mesh size. This proves convergence of the fixed-point as well as well-posedness of the system. The frictional contact-mechanical model is solved using a semi-smooth Newton algorithm based on a local nonlinear inversion of the friction rate-and-state law and a block Gauss--Seidel preconditioner exploiting the structure of the VEM-bubble-$\mathbb{P}^0$ mixed discretisation.
item.dc:creator: El Hadi Zerga, Roland Masson, Jean-Paul Ampuero, Pierre Romanet

item.title: An approximation for solutions to Helmholtz equation in polygons and its application in learning based numerical method
item.description: arXiv:2611.12506v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A learning based method for Helmholtz equations was proposed in [J. Comput. Phys. 520:113478,2025]. Based on Runge's approximation, it can be proved that when the solution can be continued outside the computational domain, using fundamental solutions as learning samples is sufficient to obtain the solution mapping with spectral accuracy. However, for complex geometries, such as domains with corners, approximation by fundamental solutions may only have logarithmic convergence due to the regularity issue, which is computationally impracticable. Moreover, approximation of a solution to the elliptic equation with those on larger domains is an ill-posed problem. In this work, we investigate how to feed additional learning samples to essentially get a practicable convergence rate and a stable algorithm, so as to ensure the generalizability of the learning based method. Error analysis and numerical examples illustrate flexibility and high-accuracy features.
item.dc:creator: Yu Chen, Jin Cheng

item.title: Investigating parameter dependence for counterexamples to Payne's nodal line conjecture using HPC
item.description: arXiv:2611.12542v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The behavior of the nodal line of the second eigenfunction of the negative Laplacian has been widely studied. Dahne could show numerically for one domain with six holes in two dimensions that it is possible to reject Payne's nodal line conjecture. We investigate the behavior of the nodal line if it does not touch the boundary, specifically the general shape, its prediction, its dependence on the parameters, and the numbers of holes. In this paper, we could address these issues numerically with a very efficient parallelized algorithm showing the rejection for various domains with six and five holes.
item.dc:creator: Sina Mattfeldt, Andreas Kleefeld

item.title: A Large Gap between Galerkin Errors with and without Mesh-Uniform Regularity for the KdV Equation with Boundary Dissipation
item.description: arXiv:2611.12585v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We compare two cubic Hermite Galerkin semidiscretizations of the Korteweg-de Vries equation on a bounded interval with boundary dissipation. They use the same trial space. The first is the weighted scheme considered in our previous paper (arXiv:2610.39269), called the W-scheme. It has mesh-uniform regularity: the discrete semigroups of the linearized equation inherit Crandall-Pazy regularity and Kato smoothing, with bounds uniform in the mesh size $h$. The second is the standard Galerkin method in $L^2$, called the S-scheme. It has no mesh-uniform regularity. For the W-scheme, the full error and the ordering error converge at an algebraic rate in $h$, uniformly on $[t_0,\infty)$ times small balls of $L^2$ for any fixed $t_0>0$. They are bounded by $Ch^p\varepsilon$ and $Ch^p\varepsilon^2$, respectively, where $\varepsilon$ is the size of the datum and $p>0$. We prove that neither bound holds for the S-scheme by using exact high-frequency spurious eigenpairs of the S-scheme. The existence of such eigenpairs for fine meshes with at least 512 elements has a proof checked by Lean 4. Computations compare the two schemes on unit-norm data built from these eigenfunctions, on 512, 1024 and 2048 elements. The full error of the S-scheme stays at $4.6\times10^{-2}$. That of the W-scheme is at most $2.2\times10^{-9}$. The ordering error of the S-scheme stays at $9.6\times10^{-6}$. That of the W-scheme falls from $2.3\times10^{-9}$ to $1.4\times10^{-10}$. Their ratio grows from $4.2\times10^3$ to $6.6\times10^4$.
item.dc:creator: Kangsheng Liu

item.title: Shape Holomorphy of the Calder\'on Projector on Lipschitz Surfaces: Frequency-Explicit Bounds for the Helmholtz
item.description: arXiv:2611.12659v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We establish the holomorphic dependence of the Calder\'on projector for the Helmholtz operator upon shape boundary deformations of a family of bounded Lipschitz domains in two and three spatial dimensions, with bounds explicit in the wavenumber and the size of the holomorphic extension. More precisely, after transporting the four boundary integral operators contained in the Calder\'on projector to a fixed reference boundary, we prove that the resulting parameter-to-operator maps admit bounded holomorphic extensions in their natural fractional Sobolev spaces. Unlike approaches that require boundary regularity of class $\mathscr C^{1,1}$ or higher, our argument traces the holomorphic dependence on the shape by transferring elliptic estimates to the boundary through the fundamental solution and the Dirichlet and conormal trace operators. This construction is the key step that allows us to treat Lipschitz-regular boundary deformations. Furthermore, we show that the domain of holomorphy can be chosen independently of the wavenumber $\kappa$, while the operator bounds in the corresponding fractional Sobolev spaces contain algebraic factors in $\kappa$ multiplied by $\exp(C\kappa\delta)$. In particular, for real domains, corresponding to $\delta=0$, our single layer estimate recovers, to our knowledge, the best available frequency dependence on general Lipschitz boundaries. For the double layer, adjoint double layer, and hypersingular operators, we obtain novel frequency-explicit bounds. The results proved in this work provide the analytic foundation for frequency-explicit uncertainty quantification, model order reduction, and high-dimensional approximation of boundary integral operators, their Galerkin discretizations, and the resulting boundary densities and quantities of interest on families of parametrically varying boundaries.
item.dc:creator: F. Henr\'iquez, J. D\"olz, J. Pinto

item.title: Stochastic Multilevel Sampling for Inverse Problems via Coarse-Space Identifiability
item.description: arXiv:2611.12667v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sampling only part of the data reduces the cost of each iteration in an inverse problem, but can make reconstruction updates unreliable. We study stochastic multilevel sampling, which computes updates on a coarse-to-fine hierarchy of correction spaces. The guiding idea is that a small sample may support a reliable coarse-grid update even when it provides insufficient information for a fine-grid update. For quadratic objectives, we identify conditions under which corrections computed from sampled data decrease the full-data objective. In small-batch experiments with computed tomography and periodic deblurring, the stochastic multilevel method improves reconstruction accuracy over matched single-level methods. In an increasingly ill-conditioned CT refinement with a fixed number of projection angles, the single-level error increases as the image dimension grows, whereas a deep hierarchy maintains or improves accuracy and outperforms full-data single-level optimization at the same number of forward and adjoint applications. The gains persist across the tested local solvers and strengthen with deeper hierarchies. A separate known-probe ptychography study provides complementary evidence for the benefit of hierarchical corrections for nonlinear inverse problems.
item.dc:creator: Zichao Wendy Di

item.title: Preconditioned Implicit Midpoint Langevin Sampling for Non-Smooth Bayesian Imaging
item.description: arXiv:2611.09980v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We introduce P-IMLA, a preconditioned implicit-midpoint Langevin sampler for high-dimensional log-concave targets with non-smooth regularization. The obstruction is that the large steps enabled by matrix preconditioning are precisely where preconditioned Euler-Maruyama inflates stationary variance. Implicit midpoint removes this surplus via a Cayley-transform identity, making P-IMLA Gaussian-exact at any step size. Beyond Gaussians, whitening transfers the sharp IMLA contraction rate to $\kappa_{\mathrm{eff}}$, and backward-error analysis gives drift-only rather than Euler-type diffusion bias under explicit smoothness assumptions. An $M$-norm Moreau envelope yields a proximal non-smooth variant with a three-term error budget. Controlled Gaussian and TV-regularized imaging experiments confirm the predicted separation: the unpreconditioned midpoint scheme retains long transients as $\kappa_f$ grows, whereas P-IMLA remains $\kappa_{\mathrm{eff}}$-governed and near variance-exact.
item.dc:creator: Sichen Wang, Zhipeng Lu

item.title: Memoryless BFGS on a nonsmooth convex function: two new results
item.description: arXiv:2611.10284v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We extend the analysis of Asl and Overton~\cite{AO2021} for memoryless BFGS (also known as L-BFGS-1) using an Armijo-Wolfe line search and applied to the nonsmooth convex function $f(x)=a|x^{(1)}|+\sum_{i=2}^n x^{(i)}$, where $n\ge2$ and $a \geq \sqrt{n-1}$. This function is unbounded below, so the method is successful if it generates function values diverging to $-\infty$, and fails otherwise. For scaled L-BFGS-1, we sharpen the sufficient condition for % az{convergence of the absolute normalized search directions} in Theorem~3.1 of failure in \cite{AO2021} from $a\ge2\sqrt{n-1}$ to $a\ge\sqrt{3(n-1)}$. For the unscaled version, we prove success for every $a$: either the method generates a direction along which no Armijo-Wolfe step exists, certifying unboundedness below, or its function values diverge to $-\infty$. Both results are consistent with the numerical experiments in \cite{AO2021}. Both proofs given here were derived with help from GPT 6 in discussions directed by the first author and corrected and rephrased afterward.
item.dc:creator: Azam Asl, Michael L. Overton

item.title: Basis selection, universal sampling discretization, and sampling recovery
item.description: arXiv:2611.10402v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: For every real $N$-dimensional subspace of $L_2$, we construct one orthonormal basis such that, for every $1\le v\le N$, at most $Cv\log(eN/v)$ positively weighted samples discretize the squared $L_2$ norm of all $v$-term combinations. Random rotations also give simultaneous weighted $L_p$ estimates and a sharp $C\log(eN)$ bound for the squared $L_2$ norm of the pointwise maximum. For prescribed coefficient classes, a change of measure yields sampling recovery estimates from $Cv\log^3(2v)$ samples under a lower Riesz inequality and a common square-integrable pointwise bound.
item.dc:creator: Feng Dai, Jiashu Ran, Vladimir N. Temlyakov

item.title: GEAR: A GPU-Accelerated Global Solver for Bounded Continuous Nonlinear Programs via Linear Bound Propagation
item.description: arXiv:2611.10487v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We present a novel GPU-accelerated global solver for constrained nonlinear programming (NLP) inspired by the efficient linear bound propagation framework in neural network (NN) verification. Existing work on NN verification, a problem that can be cast as feasibility detection for a nonlinear objective, demonstrated orders-of-magnitude speedups with the linear bound propagation-based framework when compared to traditional solvers. Extending this paradigm to global nonlinear programming requires addressing many challenges: a global constrained NLP solver must effectively exploit all, possibly unstructured, nonlinear constraints to improve the objective, whereas NN verification typically handles simple input box constraints over a well-structured NN and does not directly optimize an objective function. We address these challenges by fully exploiting the linear bounds produced by bound propagation: these linear bounds can be viewed as relaxations of nonlinear constraints and used to provide lower bounds, check infeasibility, and guide the search for a primal solution. In addition, we propose tighter linear relaxations for bilinear, quotient, and other commonly used nonlinear functions in NLP problems, and a projected augmented Lagrangian method tightly coupled to our dual solving procedure to produce primal solutions. Our method solves 421 of 505 bounded and continuous NLP problems in the GAMS and MINLPLib benchmarks under a 180-second limit, more than each of the six global solvers we compare with, including Gurobi and BARON (commercial), and SCIP (open-source). Sixteen of these problems are certified by none of the six global solvers; all of them contain exponential, logarithmic, or trigonometric terms, which are often challenging for traditional approaches. Project webpage is at https://verified-intelligence.github.io/GEAR.
item.dc:creator: Duo Zhou, Hesun Chen, Xiangru Zhong, Grani A. Hanasusanto, Huan Zhang

item.title: Reconstructing Interacting Blood Flow and Wall Interface Deformation from Noisy Flow Data Using PirateNets
item.description: arXiv:2611.10505v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Blood flow and elastic vessel-wall motion interact with each other: fluid stress drives wall deformation, while the moving wall changes the domain in which blood flows. Given noisy flow images, we study the inverse problem of reconstructing the coupled, unsteady three-dimensional motions. We solve the reconstruction through Gauss--Seidel-type alternating fluid and geometry updates. For the fluid, we use physics-informed networks to recover velocity and pressure by fitting the observations while enforcing the incompressible Navier--Stokes equations on the moving domain, which is described by an arbitrary Lagrangian--Eulerian (ALE) map. For the geometry, a reference-domain correction and sequential registration recover the vessel shape and wall displacement. Interface traction continuity and an elastic momentum equation regularize the registration so that the recovered displacement is also physics-informed. The networks evaluate fields and physical residuals at sampled space--time points without remeshing the moving domain. Experiments on a converging channel and a patient-like aorta demonstrate reconstruction of flow and wall motion from noisy data. Ablation and parameter-sensitivity studies examine the role of structure regularization and imperfect physical coefficients. A further experiment with a three-element Windkessel outlet condition demonstrates how the framework accommodates a more physiologically realistic boundary setting.
item.dc:creator: Han Zhang, Xue-Cheng Tai, Alessandro Veneziani, Raymond H. Chan

item.title: Spectral Bias Reduction in Local Gated ReLU Architectures
item.description: arXiv:2611.10700v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Neural networks trained by gradient-based methods learn the low-frequency content of a target function faster than its high-frequency content. This spectral bias is well documented, but it is much less clear which architectural choices mitigate it and which cannot. We study the question for shallow ReLU models linear in their trainable parameters, where each mode is learned at a rate given by a Gram-matrix eigenvalue, and for a general symmetric bilinear form $a(\cdot,\cdot)$, so that least-squares regression ($a=$ the $L^2$ inner product) and variational or physics-informed losses ($a=$ the $H^1$ energy form) are two instances of one analysis. Within this framework we propose gated local ReLU dictionaries, obtained by multiplying each ReLU feature by a hat partition-of-unity weight, in the spirit of partition-of-unity finite elements and overlapping Schwarz methods. The resulting Gram matrices are block-banded for any local bilinear form, with a block-Toeplitz interior whose matrix-valued symbol governs the spectrum. The two forms then behave very differently. For $L^2$ regression, the symbol is bounded away from zero, the ratio is uniform in the number of windows, and the measured spread of frequency-dependent learning rates falls from $1.9\times10^{5}$ to $4.5$ at matched model size. For the $H^1$ stiffness matrix, the symbol vanishes at zero frequency: gating leaves the $\Theta(N^2)$ conditioning intact and inverts the frequency ordering instead of removing the bias. A preconditioner built from the same interior stencil will fix the spectral bias, showing that architecture alone is not enough. Experiments on $1$D regression and Poisson problems confirm the dichotomy, and the regression effect persists when the hidden-layer parameters are trained as well.
item.dc:creator: Victorita Dolean

item.title: Improving Analytic Constants via Interpretable AI-Guided Lean Proof Refinement
item.description: arXiv:2611.10961v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: AI agents are increasingly capable of discovering new mathematical results, yet their reasoning and generated proofs can be difficult to understand and verify. We introduce an interpretable framework for AI-guided mathematical discovery, focused on improving quantitative bounds on analytic constants. Our key insight is that existing proofs often contain slack in intermediate lemmas, which can be tightened without reconstructing the entire argument. To exploit this structure, we represent proofs as partially-formalized Lean blueprints: human-interpretable dependency graphs of definitions, lemmas, and theorems. An AI agent then iteratively refines the Lean code while preserving the blueprint's dependency structure, allowing local improvements to automatically propagate to a verified final bound. This interpretable structure allows humans to inspect the agent's refinements and understand how local improvements propagate to the final theorem. For Grothendieck's constant ($\mathcal{K}_G$), we obtain $$ \mathcal{K}_G \leq \frac{\pi}{2\log(1+\sqrt{2})} - 10^{-17}, $$ an explicit numerical improvement over Krivine's 1977 bound. For Korenblum's constant ($\mathcal{K}_K$), we obtain $$ \mathcal{K}_K \geq 0.356565, $$ improving Wang's 2025 bound of $0.3554$. Our experiments demonstrate the potential of both partial formalization and iterative agentic refinement for interpretable mathematical discovery.
item.dc:creator: Rahul Saha, Alan Li, Anton Xue, Swarat Chaudhuri, Adam Klivans, Pravesh K. Kothari, Raghu Meka

item.title: Variance-Reduced Stochastic Hessian-Driven Nesterov Acceleration with Adam-Style Preconditioning
item.description: arXiv:2611.11277v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Stochastic first-order methods use sampled gradients to reduce per-iteration costs, but estimation errors can slow convergence and, in some settings, cause divergence. To improve gradient accuracy while retaining acceleration, we develop scalar and diagonal versions of VR-Adam-SHANG for smooth stochastic convex optimization. The methods combine STORM-type recursive estimation, Adam-style preconditioning, and SHANG's accelerated interpolation and correction, using at most two stochastic gradient evaluations per iteration without full-gradient refreshes. Under unbiased sampling, bounded variance, and mean-square smoothness of gradient noise, polynomial steps with prescribed initialization yield $O(1/K)$ mean-square gradient-estimation error and expected objective-gap bounds combining $O(1/K^2)$ initial-energy decay with an $O(1/\sqrt K)$ stochastic term after $K$ iterations. These guarantees require neither monotonicity of the preconditioner nor a uniform positive lower bound on its eigenvalues. The analysis also establishes polynomial-step convergence of projected nonrecursive Adam-SHANG-s, filling a gap in its original theory. Experiments compare the methods at matched sample-gradient budgets. In every tested setting, at least one of the two versions achieves the lowest mean terminal objective gap among all compared methods.
item.dc:creator: Yaxin Yu, Long Chen, Minfu Feng

item.title: Karhunen-Lo\`eve Transforms of Autoregressive Windows Based on Matched Symmetry Groups
item.description: arXiv:2611.11624v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The Karhunen-Lo\`eve transform of a window of a stationary autoregressive process of any order $p$ is described through its poles, extending the Algebraic Diversity framework, which selects a transform by the matched group. For simple roots every basis vector is a sum of at most $p$ sinusoids, at the frequencies where the spectrum equals the eigenvalue, plus modes decaying from the ends. The window covariance differs from a member of the class diagonalized by the type-II discrete cosine transform by a closed-form matrix of rank $2p$, exactly when no pole is zero, so the eigenvalues interlace spectrum samples on the cosine grid, and the coding-gain loss of the cosine transform is an exact function of that matrix with computable bounds: for the $8\times8$ Markov block of image coding at pole $0.95$ it is below 1.2 percent. By Kronecker's theorem the rank is at most $2\max(p,q)$ for rational spectra; a moving-average window departs in its Hankel corners, and an integrated (ARIMA) window departs by low rank from the type-VII sine class, exact for the random walk. The exact symmetry is generically the reflection and contains a wreath product for interleaved windows; the dihedral group of the even extension is matched approximately, the dominant pole's sign choosing cosine or sine. The two groups give the transform a fast form: a parity fold, half-length cosine cores and a cascade of at most $p$ first-order Cauchy stages, exactly $p$ for a minimal AR($p$) model. The first-order case recovers results obtained by other means.
item.dc:creator: Mitchell A. Thornton

item.title: Adjoint Kernel Sensitivity of the Rough Heston Characteristic Exponent
item.description: arXiv:2611.11652v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Multi-factor approximations of rough volatility kernels affect the characteristic exponents used in Fourier-based derivative valuation. We derive an adjoint representation for the first-order sensitivity of the rough Heston characteristic exponent with respect to its memory kernel, with model parameters and the input variance curve held fixed. The Volterra--Riccati functional $\mathcal L_T(K,z)$ admits a local real-analytic extension, jointly in the kernel perturbation and the transform parameter. The Fr\'echet derivative of this extension with respect to the kernel in $L^1$ is represented by integration against a continuous sensitivity kernel $B_K(u,z)$, obtained from a backward linear Volterra equation and independent of the perturbation direction. This representation resolves the leading-order contributions of kernel perturbations across memory lags. On the structural kernel class, which contains the fractional kernel and its multi-factor approximations and has empty interior in $L^1$, the extension yields Hadamard directional differentiability and a first-order expansion with a quadratic $L^1$-remainder for all sufficiently close structural kernels, uniformly on compact subsets of the strip of transform parameters. The same sensitivity kernel yields multi-factor weight and decay-rate derivatives. Numerical experiments at multi-factor reference kernels assess the finite-resolution implementation and illustrate how the lag distribution of positive perturbations with equal $L^1$ mass affects the first-order response.
item.dc:creator: Carlos Escudero, Francisco J. Luguera-Par\'uas, Miguel Sama

item.title: On the Global Convergence of Stochastic Adam for Physics-Informed Neural Networks
item.description: arXiv:2611.11905v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The Adam optimizer is widely used to train neural networks with highly nonlinear and nonconvex objective functions. Remarkably, Adam often drives the empirical training loss nearly to zero. This phenomenon has been partially explained by neural tangent kernel (NTK) analyses of gradient descent (GD) and stochastic gradient descent (SGD). However, analyzing Adam presents additional challenges. Its first-moment momentum couples stochastic gradients across iterations, while its adaptive second-moment preconditioner depends on the same stochastic gradient used in the update. In this paper, we establish linear convergence guarantees for Adam in training sufficiently wide two-layer neural networks with either full-batch or minibatch gradients. For full-batch Adam, we construct a Lyapunov function to control the effect of historical momentum. For minibatch Adam, our analysis builds on an exact virtual-iterate representation, a conditional analysis of the dependence between stochastic gradients and adaptive preconditioners, and uniform concentration bounds for the second-moment estimates. We prove geometric decay of the empirical loss for full-batch Adam and geometric decay in restricted expectation on a high-probability event for minibatch Adam. Beyond regression, we extend our convergence analysis to physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) for solving the Poisson equation, where differential operators and separate sampling of interior and boundary points introduce additional challenges. We establish analogous global convergence guarantees for both deterministic and stochastic Adam under explicit conditions on network width and Adam's parameters, characterizing the effects of minibatch size on convergence. These results help bridge the gap between Adam's empirical success and its theoretical understanding, providing sharper convergence guarantees for PINNs than existing analyses.
item.dc:creator: Yihang Gao

item.title: Online Digital Twins: Data Assimilation and Control
item.description: arXiv:2611.12001v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The online assimilation of data and the application of controls are essential ingredients of the digital twin paradigm. In this paper, we formalize the online interaction between the physical process and its virtual digital representation in the setting of continuously arriving data from the physical process and a receding horizon virtual planning process, which provides the control for the physical process. Our mathematical formulation relies on a mean field representation of the data assimilation process as well as a mean field Pontryagin minimum principle for the optimal control problem. Such mean field formulations are computationally attractive because they allow for simultaneous implementation in terms of Hamiltonian interacting particle systems. A more detailed discussion is included for the ensemble Kalman-Bucy filter in combination with affine approximations of the receding horizon control laws. This paper sets out the mathematical framework, while a computational study is left for future research.
item.dc:creator: Sebastian Reich

item.title: Parametric spatio-temporal reduced-order modelling via Spectral Proper Orthogonal Decomposition and Gaussian Process Regression
item.description: arXiv:2611.12028v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We present SPOD-GPR, a non-intrusive, parametric, spatio-temporal reduced-order model (ROM) that combines Proper Orthogonal Decomposition (POD), Spectral POD (SPOD), and Gaussian Process Regression (GPR). A parametric POD first projects the high-dimensional state onto a low-dimensional subspace. The reduced trajectories are then divided into windowed sections, transformed into the frequency domain, and truncated to the most energetic frequencies. SPOD is then performed independently at each retained frequency, yielding temporally coherent modes and coefficients. The parametric dependence of the POD and SPOD bases is modelled by GPR on a local chart of the Grassmann manifold after Procrustes alignment. The SPOD modal coefficients are learned both as explicit functions of the parameters and through a parameter-conditioned autoregressive model that allows for temporal extrapolation beyond the training window. Gaussian processes are sampled jointly and pathwise via Matheron conditioning, ensuring that each predictive realization carries uncertainty quantification consistent with the posterior distribution. The method is tested on four parametric examples where the parameter values and the prediction horizon lie outside the training data: the two-dimensional anisotropic Kuramoto--Sivashinsky equation in a time-periodic and a travelling-wave regime, each parametrised by one of its two coefficients; flow past a cylinder parametrised by the Reynolds number; and flow past an elliptic obstacle parametrised by its semi-axes. In all cases, SPOD-GPR reduces the normalised mean absolute error compared to a POD-GPR baseline, and improves the calibration of the predictive uncertainty, especially in the fluid flow cases, where POD-GPR is severely overconfident. This opens the way to spectral, uncertainty-aware reduced-order models for many-query and real-time applications, such as digital twins.
item.dc:creator: Guglielmo Padula, Antonio Colanera, Gianluigi Rozza

item.title: Same Physics, Different Gradients: A State-of-the-Art Report on Differentiable Physics Simulation
item.description: arXiv:2611.12162v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Differentiable simulation propagates derivatives through a physics simulator, turning animation, system identification, control, and computational design into gradient-based optimization. Engines differ in the physics they model and, less visibly, in which mathematical object they differentiate. We separate two questions the literature conflates. The referent is which object the returned derivative belongs to: the finite computation that executed, the converged equation it approximates, or the continuous dynamics. The realization describes the organization of the backward pass: automatically generated differentiation, an equation-level adjoint solve, or a custom adjoint. The referent defines the target against which exactness is assessed; the implementation determines how accurately that target is approximated. Cost depends on the realization together with how the states needed by the backward pass are retained or recovered. Crossing the axes places every method and engine we classify in a cell, separates claims the literature merges, and shows that the apparent trade-off between exactness and memory follows from how methods have been built rather than from a constraint. A second, orthogonal taxonomy covers contact, where the map is non-smooth. We then ask whether a correct gradient helps. Four mechanisms by which useful gradients are lost are cataloged and measured on one testbed, where the advantage of the exact derivative over the equation-level adjoint depends on where the fitting target comes from as much as on the solver budget, and we review the evidence that zeroth-order methods can outperform simulator gradients in the regimes where those mechanisms act. The model classes, systems techniques and applications are surveyed through this lens, and we close with a reporting checklist, a released diagnostic that computes it, and a research agenda.
item.dc:creator: Lei Shu, Zizhou Huang, Yunuo Chen, Yifei Li, Tao Du, Minchen Li, Tuur Stuyck, Miles Macklin, Kui Wu, Bo Zhu, Yin Yang, Ming C. Lin, Alberta Longhini, Rika Antonova, Leonidas Guibas, Gordon Wetzstein, Jeannette Bohg, Chenfanfu Jiang

item.title: Amortized Transport-Map Likelihoods for Hierarchical Inverse Problems with Application to Wetting
item.description: arXiv:2611.12193v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Hierarchical Bayesian models pool measurements, but with the forward model in the likelihood every posterior evaluation costs one forward solve per cell. To reduce this cost, we introduce a simulation-based inference framework in which a triangular transport-map likelihood, trained once per design, serves every cell. We apply it to infer wetting properties from photographs of a stable hole in a thin liquid film. The hole's radius depends, through the nonlinear Young-Laplace equation, on the contact angle and capillary length. One photograph gives rank-one information about them, so we pool many in a hierarchical model whose cells, each a substrate at one volume setting, share the apparatus geometry and the noise scale. A design fixes the number of substrates, the volume settings and the photographs per cell. The map's posteriors agree with direct sampling of the forward model in the wetting properties at a synthetic validation design, and less closely at a larger synthetic scaling design. At the validation design, simulation-based calibration detects no departure for any parameter. There, the map needs several hundred times fewer forward-model evaluations than direct sampling with a gradient-free ensemble sampler for a single posterior, and about five orders of magnitude fewer over a calibration study of 200 posteriors. On real photographs its posterior agrees with direct sampling and is consistent with the measured radii. Trained offline, the amortized map turns new photographs into a posterior with no forward solve. It is thus a major step toward measuring wetting properties in situ without disturbing the liquid.
item.dc:creator: Henning Bonart

item.title: Certified finite-precision readout for $p$-adic kernel aggregation
item.description: arXiv:2611.12254v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In non-archimedean numerical analysis, a verified $p$-adic approximation can determine an absolute value, and hence downstream probabilistic rankings and classification decisions, with mathematical exactness long before the underlying number is fully resolved. We turn this observation into rigorous finite-precision certificates for norm-based readouts of amplitude families. For a common error radius, a nonempty resolved set already fixes every exact maximizer, ties included, at the sharp integer absolute precision $v_*+1$, and conditioning on that set yields an exact total-variation identity separating unresolved $p$-adic mass from real rounding error. For aggregates of $p$-adic exponentials, we give a centered-moment certificate with an explicit remainder bound: on rational data it runs in exact rational arithmetic without individual exponential evaluations, attains its minimal bound at an active phase, and resolves every nonzero aggregate at high order; we also obtain an aggregate perturbation bound free of summand-count factors.
